pillar_reactions.evidence: He had pre-sold himself on the feedback loop before it was presented, tying it to his own competitive instinct: 'it's week by week, and then sending in videos, timing the sessions, then pushing it... that week by week, getting better, getting feedback, and trying to beat your last record. It's like a very competitive sort of sport-like aspect that I enjoy.' On being asked to score the offer he named this pillar first: 'the training mobility, the weekly adjustments, that's what I would like to have.' This is the component he wanted and the only one he was still buying at the end of the call.

Strong immediate reaction to the no-tracking promise, tied directly to his own history: 'The nutrition, no counting macros, is very attractive to me because I've always counted calories and macros, so you guys saying you don't need to have that is interesting. I'm assuming it's like the carnivore diet, which is great, to not count. I wonder what more that would look like.' The reaction reversed within six minutes once price landed and he re-scoped himself: 'the nutrition, like I know how to get shredded' — enthusiasm for the mechanism, no willingness to pay for it.

One question, and it was about capacity rather than value: 'how many people on average do you see are in the...?' He was told 289 in Primal University and 30 in one-to-one coaching with Trevor. He never engaged with the personal-phone-number promise, the community, or the coach relationship at all, and this pillar did not appear in his reasons for scoring the offer a five or six.

anchors.raw: I can get there pretty quickly if I just do the bodybuilding stuff, cutting, eating 1,800, 1,700 calories.
anchors.note: The decisive anchor on this call. His alternative is free, self-administered, and demonstrably worked — he reached 7-8% body fat with it six months ago. Reinforced twice more: 'I could probably do it myself, it'll just take longer' and 'I know how to get shredded.' No amount of programme quality overcomes an anchor of zero dollars for a proven personal result, and the rep never tried to price the 'it'll just take longer' against anything.

anchors.raw: I wanted to see more $2,000 to $2,500 for three months.
anchors.note: A rare gift — an explicit counter-price rather than a vague objection, given unprompted seconds after the tiers were read. It places his expectation at roughly 55-60% of the three-month list price. Nothing in the offer structure reaches it, and the rep never asked what produced the number.

anchors.raw: I like to have a trainer almost at all times, just because it allows me to like learn something new and like learn it the right way... So like bodybuilding, I had a trainer for like a year and a half. And then same thing with like calisthenics, same thing with like basketball.
anchors.note: The strongest supportive anchor available and it was left on the table. He buys coaching as a standing habit, has done so across three separate disciplines, and frames it as how he learns anything new. The rep never asked what any of those trainers cost, which would have established both a payment norm and a comparison the $6,000 could be positioned against.

anchors.raw: What do you think about the monthly basic plan? Will that at least... it's $200.
anchors.note: The prospect asked for the cheaper own-brand tier by name and by price before the rep offered it, having found it himself. Once he learned it contained actual form videos rather than PDFs — 'I didn't know that this was that in-depth' — the $6,000 offer had no route back.

unmet_demand.want: Form coaching on kettlebells alone, without paying for nutrition he does not need
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The offer is an indivisible bundle of three pillars and there is no form-only or training-only tier at any price between $200/mo and $4,000. He stated the scope precisely — 'the biggest thing I care about is form... I just don't know how to safely throw a kettlebell around' — and the only product matching it is the one with no form review in it.

unmet_demand.want: Actual form feedback on his kettlebell technique given his bad shoulders, at a price he would pay
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The film-and-review loop exists only in the one-to-one tier he was priced out of. Primal University was presented as containing 'step-by-step guides', 'technique breakdowns' and 'a little bit of accountability', and he left believing it answers his safety need. Nobody said plainly that nobody will watch him lift. For a prospect with disclosed shoulder problems this is the gap with real-world consequences, not just commercial ones.

unmet_demand.want: A three-month engagement in the $2,000-2,500 range
unmet_demand.why_unmet: No tier exists there. The nearest options are $1,200 for one month or $4,000 for three, and the financing routes carry unquoted interest on top rather than reducing the total.

unmet_demand.want: Training that integrates with basketball and actively preserves athleticism rather than sitting alongside it
unmet_demand.why_unmet: This was his stated reason for leaving bodybuilding — 'it's a whole other routine you have to do, it's not intertwined with the workout splits' — and the mobility pillar almost certainly answers it. It was delivered as generic anti-sitting messaging about brushing your teeth and waking up fluid, and never connected to his sport, his hips or his court performance.

unmet_demand.want: Financing terms he could evaluate — rate, total and schedule
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He asked directly, 'Is that interest-free or no?', and received 'A little bit of interest on each' with no rate and no figures. He could not price the option, so he discounted it and moved on within one turn: 'That's tough. This is out of what I was expecting.'
